Blowup behavior of strongly perturbed wave equationsThanks: Both authors are supported by the Austrian Science Fund FWF, Project P 30076: “Self-similar blowup in dispersive wave equations”.

Roland Donninger Address: Universität Wien, Fakultät für Mathematik, Oskar-Morgenstern-Platz 1, 1090 Vienna, Austria Email address: roland.donninger@univie.ac.at and David Wallauch Address: Universität Wien, Fakultät für Mathematik, Oskar-Morgenstern-Platz 1, 1090 Vienna, Austria Email address: david.wallauch@univie.ac.at
Abstract.

We study the blowup behavior of a class of strongly perturbed wave equations with a focusing supercritical power nonlinearity in three spatial dimensions. We show that the ODE blowup profile of the unperturbed equation still describes the asymptotics of stable blowup. As a consequence, stable ODE-type blowup is seen to be a universal phenomenon that exists in a large class of semilinear wave equations.

1. Introduction

Nonlinear wave equations describe a wide variety of phenomena in fields ranging from fundamental physics to the applied sciences, e.g. general relativity, quantum field theory, solid state physics, and nonlinear optics. Typically, the equations that occur in applications are way too complicated for a rigorous mathematical analysis. One therefore resorts to toy models that are supposed to capture and isolate essential features of the more complicated equations. From the point of view of applications this strategy is only meaningful if the phenomena discovered in the toy model are stable under perturbations of the equation.

In the present paper we focus on the formation of singularities (or blowup) in finite time. The basic semilinear wave equation

□u(t,x):=(∂t2−Δx)u(t,x)=u(t,x)|u(t,x)|p−1,p>1\Box u(t,x):=(\partial_{t}^{2}-\Delta_{x})u(t,x)=u(t,x)|u(t,x)|^{p-1},\quad p>1

admits the explicit ODE blowup given by

u⁡(t,x)=(2​(p+1)(p−1)2)1p−1​(1−t)−2p−1,u(t,x)=\left(\frac{2(p+1)}{(p-1)^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}(1-t)^{-\frac{2}{p-1}},

which is known to be stable under perturbations of the initial data [18, 19, 8]. It is thus natural to ask whether this type of blowup is also relevant for more complicated equations that occur in applications. In this paper we show that the stable ODE blowup persists if one perturbs the equation in a very general way. Roughly speaking, we consider equations of the form

□​u+F⁡(u,∂u)=u​|u|p−1\Box u+F(u,\partial u)=u|u|^{p-1}

where FF is (at most) linear in the derivatives ∂u\partial u and satisfies some mild, natural requirements. We do not impose any smallness assumption on FF. Our result covers the whole range p>3p>3 in 33 space dimensions and we allow for complex-valued solutions. A random example of an equation that we can cover would be

□​u​(t,x)+t5​ei​t+|x|2​u​(t,x)​∂tu⁡(t,x)+u​(t,x)6=u⁡(t,x)​|u⁡(t,x)|6.\Box u(t,x)+t^{5}e^{it+|x|^{2}}u(t,x)\partial_{t}u(t,x)+u(t,x)^{6}=u(t,x)|u(t,x)|^{6}.

For the sake of simplicity we restrict ourselves to radial solutions but the extension to the general case is purely technical.

The mechanism we exploit is most easily explained by considering the Klein-Gordon equation

□​u+m​u=u​|u|p−1.\Box u+mu=u|u|^{p-1}.

The natural scaling transform related to the pure wave case (m=0m=0) is given by

u⁡(t,x)↦uλ​(t,x):=λ−2p−1​u​(tλ,xλ).u(t,x)\mapsto u_{\lambda}(t,x):=\lambda^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}u\left(\tfrac{t}{\lambda},\tfrac{x}{\lambda}\right).

Under this scaling, the Klein-Gordon equation transforms as

□​uλ+λ2​pp−1​m​uλ=uλ​|uλ|p−1\Box u_{\lambda}+\lambda^{\frac{2p}{p-1}}mu_{\lambda}=u_{\lambda}|u_{\lambda}|^{p-1}

and if λ→0\lambda\to 0, the mass term becomes negligible. The ODE blowup is self-similar and effectively, the solution moves to smaller and smaller scales as the blowup time is approached. The heuristic scaling analysis therefore suggests that the mass term (and much more general perturbations) can be neglected close to the blowup time. We implement this idea rigorously by a purely perturbative argument. Consequently, we do not make use of fragile structural properties like Lyapunov functionals or virial identities. That is why we are able to treat very general perturbations and all p>3p>3. Our result shows, for the first time in the supercritical context, that stable ODE blowup is a universal phenomenon that occurs in a large class of models.

1.1. Setup

Since we restrict ourselves to the radial case, the effective Cauchy problem we study is given by

{(∂t2−∂r2−2r∂r)u(t,r)+F(t,r,u(t,r),∂tu(t,r),∂ru(t,r))=|u(t,r)|p−1u(t,r)u⁡(T0,r)=f⁡(r)∂0u⁡(T0,r)=g⁡(r),\begin{cases}&\left(\partial_{t}^{2}-\partial_{r}^{2}-\frac{2}{r}\partial_{r}\right)u(t,r)+F(t,r,u(t,r),\partial_{t}u(t,r),\partial_{r}u(t,r))=|u(t,r)|^{p-1}u(t,r)\\ &u(T_{0},r)=f(r)\\ &\partial_{0}u(T_{0},r)=g(r),\end{cases} (1.1)

where T0T_{0} is some initial time which we will specify below. Furthermore, pp is a constant that satisfies 3<p3<p. We additionally assume that ff and gg are complex-valued initial data and that FF satisfies some natural constraints. Note that in the unperturbed case (F=0)(F=0), Eq. (1.1) has a conserved energy given by

ℰ(u(t,.),∂tu(t,.))=12∥(u(t,.),∂tu(t,.)∥(H˙1×L2)​(ℝ3)2−1p−1∥u(t,.)∥Lp+1​(ℝ3)p+1.\mathcal{E}(u(t,.),\partial_{t}u(t,.))=\frac{1}{2}\|(u(t,.),\partial_{t}u(t,.)\|^{2}_{(\dot{H}^{1}\times L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{3})}-\frac{1}{p-1}\|u(t,.)\|^{p+1}_{L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}.

Under the transformation

u⁡(t,r)↦uλ​(t,r):=λ−2p−1​u​(tλ,rλ)u(t,r)\mapsto u_{\lambda}(t,r):=\lambda^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}u\left(\frac{t}{\lambda},\frac{r}{\lambda}\right)

this energy scales as

ℰ(uλ(t,.),∂tuλ(t,.))=λp−5p−1ℰ(u(t,.),∂tu(t,.)),\mathcal{E}(u_{\lambda}(t,.),\partial_{t}u_{\lambda}(t,.))=\lambda^{\frac{p-5}{p-1}}\mathcal{E}(u(t,.),\partial_{t}u(t,.)),

while Eq. (1.1) remains invariant if it is unperturbed. Therefore, we say that Eq. (1.1) is subcritical for 1<p<51<p<5, critical for p=5p=5, and supercritical for p>5p>5.
We also remark that by employing the wave propagators cos⁡(t​|∇|)\cos(t|\nabla|) and sin⁡(t​|∇|)|∇|\frac{\sin(t|\nabla|)}{|\nabla|}, a weak formulation of Eq. (1.1) is given by

u⁡(t,r)=\displaystyle u(t,r)= cos⁡(t​|∇|)​f+sin⁡(t​|∇|)|∇|​g+∫0tsin⁡((t−s)​|∇|)|∇|​𝒩​(u)​(s,r)​𝑑s,\displaystyle\cos(t|\nabla|)f+\frac{\sin(t|\nabla|)}{|\nabla|}g+\int_{0}^{t}\frac{\sin((t-s)|\nabla|)}{|\nabla|}\mathcal{N}(u)(s,r)ds,

where

𝒩⁡(u)​(s,r)=(|u⁡(s,r)|p−1​u​(s,r)−F⁡(s,r,u⁡(s,r),∂su⁡(s,r),∂ru⁡(s,r))).\mathcal{N}(u)(s,r)=(|u(s,r)|^{p-1}u(s,r)-F(s,r,u(s,r),\partial_{s}u(s,r),\partial_{r}u(s,r))).

This weak formulation now has the advantage that instead of having to deal with the differential equation itself, one obtains a fixed point problem. In order to be able to find a fixed point, it is vital to work in a space with enough regularity to control the (possibly) supercritical nonlinearity. In our case H2×H1H^{2}\times H^{1} will be sufficient. Recall that for F=0F=0, Eq. (1.1) has an explicit blow up solution given by

uT​(t,r)=κp​(T−t)−2p−1u^{T}(t,r)=\kappa_{p}(T-t)^{-\frac{2}{p-1}} (1.2)

where

κp=(2​(p+1)(p−1)2)1p−1.\kappa_{p}=\left(\frac{2(p+1)}{(p-1)^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}.

For notational convenience we further set cp=κpp−1c_{p}=\kappa_{p}^{p-1}. Note that since we allow for complex-valued solutions, the phase shift u↦ei​θ​uu\mapsto e^{i\theta}u, θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}, is another symmetry that leaves the unperturbed equation invariant. This leads to a two parameter family of blowup solutions given by

uθT:=ei​θ​uT.u^{T}_{\theta}:=e^{i\theta}u^{T}.

Our interest in complex-valued solutions stems from the fact that, as a special case of Eq. (1.1), we obtain a semilinear Klein-Gordon equation.

Now we turn or attention to the perturbation term F⁡(t,r,u⁡(t,r),∂tu⁡(t,r),∂ru⁡(t,r))F(t,r,u(t,r),\partial_{t}u(t,r),\partial_{r}u(t,r)). First of all, we assume FF to be of the form

F⁡(t,r,u,v,w)=A⁡(t,r,u)+B⁡(t,r,u)​v+C⁡(t,r,u)​w,F(t,r,u,v,w)=A(t,r,u)+B(t,r,u)v+C(t,r,u)w, (1.3)

|A⁡(t,r,u)|≤M⁡(1+|u|q)|A⁡(t,r,u1)−A⁡(t,r,u2)|≤M​|u1​|u1|q−1−u2​|u2|q−1|.\begin{split}|A(t,r,u)|&\leq M(1+|u|^{q})\\ |A(t,r,u_{1})-A(t,r,u_{2})|&\leq M\left|u_{1}|u_{1}|^{q-1}-u_{2}|u_{2}|^{q-1}\right|.\end{split} (1.5)

|∂rF⁡(t,r,u,v,w)|≤M⁡(1+|u|q+|v|+|w|)|∂xF⁡(t,r,x+i​y,v,w)|+|∂yF⁡(t,r,x+i​y,v,w)|≤M⁡(1+|u|q−1+|v|+|w|).\begin{split}|\partial_{r}F(t,r,u,v,w)|\leq&M(1+|u|^{q}+|v|+|w|)\\ |\partial_{x}F(t,r,x+iy,v,w)|+|\partial_{y}F(t,r,x+iy,v,w)|\leq&M(1+|u|^{q-1}+|v|+|w|).\end{split} (1.6)

1.2. Related results

The study of blowup solutions for semilinear wave equations has attracted a lot of interest in recent years and due to the sheer volume of results, we only mention a handful of works that deal with ODE-type blowup. In the unperturbed case, many results concerning the stability of the ODE blowup are available. The subcritical case was thoroughly studied by Merle and Zaag [18, 19, 25], see also the work by Alexakis and Shao [1] and Azaiez [2]. Furthermore, in the one-dimensional case, Merle and Zaag were able to give a fairly complete picture of the blowup behavior [20, 21, 22, 26]. They also managed to extend some of these results to higher dimensions [23, 24]. In the supercritical case, a very influential numerical paper is [3] by Bizoń, Chmaj, and Tabor. Rigorous results were established in [7] and [8] by the first author and Schörkhuber. Recently, the stability for the critical equation in three and five dimensions was shown in optimal regularity by proving Strichartz estimates [4, 6]. In the subcritical case, Hamza et. al. [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15] studied the blowup behavior under various perturbations of the equation, see also the paper by Killip, Stovall, and Visan [17] on blowup bounds for the Klein-Gordon equation. Very recently, Speck [28] studied ODE-type blowup in a class of quasilinear wave equations.

With these preliminaries out of the way we will now analyze the linear part of Eq. (1.11). To do so, we define the space ℋ\mathcal{H} as

This setup now enables us to show that the unbounded operator corresponding to the linear part in (1.11), equipped with a proper domain, is closable and that its closure generates a C0C_{0}-semigroup. To that end we define the operator L~\tilde{\textup{{L}}} with

The operator L~:D⁡(L~)→ℋ\tilde{\textup{{L}}}:D(\tilde{\textup{{L}}})\to\mathcal{H} is closable and its closure L generates a C0C_{0}-semigroup S:[0,∞)→ℬ⁡(ℋ)\textup{{S}}:[0,\infty)\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}\right) with

‖S​(τ)‖≲e−2p−1​τ.\|\textup{{S}}(\tau)\|\lesssim e^{-\frac{2}{p-1}\tau}. (2.1)

Lemma 2.5.

The eigenvalues 0 and 1 both have geometric multiplicity 1. Furthermore the geometric eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue 00 is spanned by r0\textup{{r}}_{0} while the other one is spanned by g0,\textup{{g}}_{0}, with

r0​(ρ):=(0012p−1)​a​n​dg0​(ρ):=(1p+1p−100).\textup{{r}}_{0}(\rho):=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\\ 1\\ \frac{2}{p-1}\end{pmatrix}\;\;and\quad\textup{{g}}_{0}(\rho):=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \frac{p+1}{p-1}\\ 0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}.

Assume that there is another eigenfunction r~​(ρ)\tilde{\textup{{r}}}(\rho). This would then imply that r~4​(ρ)=2p−1​r~3​(ρ)+ρ​r~3​(ρ)\tilde{r}_{4}(\rho)=\frac{2}{p-1}\tilde{r}_{3}(\rho)+\rho\tilde{r}_{3}(\rho) and that r~​(ρ)=ρ​r~3\tilde{r}(\rho)=\rho\tilde{r}_{3} satisfies

Now any solution of Eq. (2.10) has to be a linear combination of these two solutions. ‖Sθ​(τ)​P~θ​u‖≲e−43​(p−1)​τ​‖P~θ​u‖\|\textup{{S}}_{\theta}(\tau)\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta}\textup{{u}}\|\lesssim e^{-\frac{4}{3(p-1)}\tau}\|\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta}\textup{{u}}\|

3.1. Estimates on the nonlinearity

The first important estimate of the nonlinear theory is the following.

These two Lemmas will be vital for the fixed point argument which will be done later on. We continue by employing Duhamel’s Principle, to rewrite Eq. (2.6) as an integral equation, which, for any initial data Φ⁡(0)=u∈ℋ\Phi(0)=\textup{{u}}\in\mathcal{H}, takes the form

To analyse this equation further, we need the correct functional analytic setting and therefore introduce the two Banach spaces (𝒳,∥.∥𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\|.\|_{\mathcal{X}}) and (X,∥.∥X)(X,\|.\|_{X}) as follows.

Set 𝒳:={Φ∈C⁡([0,∞),ℋ):‖Φ‖𝒳<∞}\mathcal{X}:=\{\Phi\in C([0,\infty),\mathcal{H}):\|\Phi\|_{\mathcal{X}}<\infty\}, with

The second Banach space that will be needed is the following.

Let δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 be small enough and T0∈[1−3​δc,1−2​δc]T_{0}\in[1-\frac{3\delta}{c},1-\frac{2\delta}{c}] as well as T∈[1−δc,1+δc]T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c},1+\frac{\delta}{c}] where c≥1c\geq 1. Then, provided cc is chosen large enough, we have the estimates

4.4. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Proof.

Theorem 1.1 is now essentially a consequence of the last few Lemmas. Therefore let δ,T0,\delta,T_{0}, and cc, be as in the assumptions of Lemma 4.4 and suppose that the initial data (f,g)(f,g) of Eq. (1.1) satisfy the conditions of Theorem 1.1. Then, by the previous Lemma, there exists a T∈[1−δc2,1+δc2]T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] as well as functions (Φ,θ)∈𝒳δ×Xδ(\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} which solve Eq. (3.2) with initial data Φ​(0)=U​(T,v)\Phi(0)=\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}), where v:=(f~,g~)\textup{{v}}:=(\tilde{f},\tilde{g}) is as in 1.12. Hence, Ψ⁡(τ):=Φ⁡(τ)+Ψθ⁡(τ)\Psi(\tau):=\Phi(\tau)+\Psi_{\theta(\tau)} satisfies Eq. (2.2) in the mild sense, with initial data Ψ⁡(0)=Ψ0+U⁡(T,v)\Psi(0)=\Psi_{0}+U(T,\textup{{v}}). By undoing the transformations done in the first section, we obtain that

solves the original perturbed radial wave equation (1.1) with initial data

We thus calculate

≲\displaystyle\lesssim (T−t)12∥Ψθ∞−Ψ(−log(T−t)+log(T−T0),.T−t))∥ℋ⁡(𝔹T−t3)\displaystyle(T-t)^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\Psi_{\theta_{\infty}}-\Psi(-\log(T-t)+\log(T-T_{0}),\frac{.}{T-t}))\|_{\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{T-t})}
≤\displaystyle\leq ∥Ψθ∞−Ψ(−log(T−t)+log(T−T0),.)∥\displaystyle\|\Psi_{\theta_{\infty}}-\Psi(-\log(T-t)+\log(T-T_{0}),.)\|
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖Ψθ∞−Ψθ⁡(−log⁡(T−t)+log⁡(T−T0))‖\displaystyle\|\Psi_{\theta_{\infty}}-\Psi_{\theta(-\log(T-t)+\log(T-T_{0}))}\|
+|(Φ(−log(T−t)+log(T−T0))∥\displaystyle+|(\Phi(-\log(T-t)+\log(T-T_{0}))\|

for all t∈[T0,T).t\in[T_{0},T). As the other stated bounds follow analogously, the proof of Theorem 1.1 is completed. ∎
